passages.t: Two armies, and a champion from Gath
passages.happening:
The Philistines gather at Socoh in Judah and camp between Socoh and Azekah. Saul and Israel camp in the Valley of Elah. ‘The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites stood on another, with the valley between them’ (verse 3).

A champion comes out from the Philistine camp, Goliath of Gath. He is six cubits and a span tall, with a bronze helmet, a coat of bronze armor weighing five thousand shekels, bronze on his legs, a bronze javelin on his back, and a spear with a shaft like a weaver's beam (verses 4-7).

He shouts to Israel's ranks: “Choose one of your men and have him come down against me” (verse 8). If the man can kill him, the Philistines will serve Israel. If Goliath wins, Israel will serve them (verse 9). “I defy the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man to fight!” (verse 10).

“On hearing the words of the Philistine, Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The Valley of Elah runs west from the hill country of Judah toward the Philistine plain, a natural road for the Philistines to push inland. Socoh and Azekah are known sites above the valley. Gath, Goliath's city, is usually placed at Tell es-Safi, where excavations have found a large Philistine city. Nearby, the fortified town of Khirbet Qeiyafa, excavated from 2007, dates to roughly the time of Saul and David. Its excavators proposed that it was the Shaaraim of verse 52, but that is debated.

Single combat between champions was known in the ancient world, a way to decide a battle, or at least to shame the other side, without a full clash of armies. The word for champion is used only in this chapter. It means the man of the between, the one who steps into the space between two armies.

Goliath's armor is described in unusual detail. The coat alone weighed roughly 125 pounds. The detail is meant to impress, and it also shows the Philistine advantage in metal that chapter 13 described.

His height has a history in the text. The standard Hebrew gives six cubits and a span, about nine and a half feet. The Dead Sea Scroll copy of Samuel and the Greek translation read four cubits and a span, about six feet nine inches, still a giant among the men of his day.

The chapter opens with a wide view of two armies on two hills, then narrows to one giant. And the tall king, chosen to go out before Israel and fight its battles, is as afraid as everyone else.
passages.later: Another verse names a different man in connection with Goliath. In the standard Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19, Elhanan of Bethlehem kills ‘Goliath the Gittite’, while Chronicles says that Elhanan killed ‘Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite’ (1 Chronicles 20:5). The Berean Standard Bible supplies the brother of in 2 Samuel 21:19 from Chronicles. Scholars explain the relation of these texts in different ways, and the site's page on the numbers in Samuel, Kings and Chronicles sets them out.
passages.asks: Saul and all Israel heard the giant and were afraid. Ask what voice in your life keeps coming out morning and evening to frighten you. And ask what you have let it name as the measure of your strength.

passages.t: A boy with bread and cheese
passages.happening:
David is the youngest of Jesse's eight sons. His three eldest brothers, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, have followed Saul to war, while David goes back and forth from Saul to tend his father's sheep in Bethlehem (verses 12-15). ‘For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand’ (verse 16).

Jesse sends David to the camp with roasted grain and ten loaves for his brothers, and ten cheeses for their commander (verses 17-18). David arrives as the army is going out to its battle line, leaves his supplies, and runs to find his brothers (verses 20-22). While he is talking with them, Goliath comes out and shouts his usual words, and David hears him (verse 23). The men of Israel run from him in fear (verse 24).

The soldiers tell one another of the king's reward: great riches, his daughter in marriage, and freedom from taxes for the man's family (verse 25). David asks, “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (verse 26).

His eldest brother Eliab hears him and is angry. He asks why David has come and with whom he left ‘those few sheep in the wilderness’, and accuses him of pride (verse 28). “What have I done now?” said David. “Was it not just a question?” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Forty days of the same challenge, morning and evening, shows how stuck Israel was.

The key word of the chapter is defy, or taunt. Goliath uses it of Israel's ranks. David uses it of ‘the armies of the living God’. What the soldiers hear as a threat to Israel, David hears as an insult to God. A related word is translated disgrace in verse 26. The whole contest is a question of honor: whose God will be shamed?

David calls the LORD the living God, set against Philistine gods that cannot act. Calling Goliath uncircumcised marked him as outside the covenant, since circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's family.

The king's reward, riches, a royal marriage and freedom from taxes, was the kind of favor a champion could expect. David asks about it, and he also asks the larger question.

Eliab was the son Samuel had thought must be the LORD's anointed, and the LORD had said no (16:6-7). Now the youngest is asking questions at the front.
passages.later: The title the living God was used when Israel first crossed into the land: ‘This is how you will know that the living God is among you’ (Joshua 3:10).
passages.asks: David asked who this Philistine was, to defy the armies of the living God. Ask what difference it makes to see a threat as an insult to God and not only to you. And ask whether you have answered a younger person's honest question with the scorn Eliab showed.

passages.t: Lions, bears, and the name of the LORD
passages.happening:
David's words reach Saul, and he is brought in. “Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!” (verse 32). Saul answers that he is just a boy, and Goliath has been a warrior from his youth (verse 33).

David tells him what he has done as a shepherd. When a lion or a bear took a lamb, he went after it, struck it down and rescued the lamb (verses 34-35). “The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine” (verse 37). “Go,” said Saul, “and may the LORD be with you.”

Saul dresses David in his own tunic, helmet and armor. David tries to walk and cannot. “I cannot walk in these,” David said to Saul. “I am not accustomed to them” (verse 39). He takes them off. With his staff in his hand he chooses five smooth stones from the stream, puts them in his shepherd's bag, and goes toward the Philistine with his sling (verse 40).

Goliath sees a boy and despises him. “Am I a dog,” he said to David, “that you come at me with sticks?” He curses David by his gods (verse 43).

David answers: “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied” (verse 45). The whole world will know ‘that there is a God in Israel’ (verse 46). “And all those assembled here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands” (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
David's courage rests on what God has already done. The LORD who rescued him from the lion and the bear will rescue him now. In this chapter faith is memory put to work in a new danger.

Saul's armor is the armor of the man who should have fought. It does not fit the boy, and David goes out as what he is, a shepherd.

The sling was not a child's toy. Trained slingers were a regular part of ancient armies. The book of Judges tells of seven hundred left-handed men of Benjamin who could sling a stone at a hair without missing. A smooth stone thrown hard could kill at a distance, and a shepherd used a sling to defend the flock.

David's words in verses 45 to 47 are the center of the chapter. Goliath curses by his gods. David speaks in the name of the LORD of Hosts. He says before the stone is thrown why he will win, and he gives the reason to the whole world.

The story is often read as a lesson in believing in oneself, as if the point were that brave small people can beat big strong ones. The text says the opposite. David wins because he is not trusting himself at all. He trusts the God whose name Goliath insulted.
passages.later:
The book of Judges describes the skill of Israel's slingers: ‘each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing’ (Judges 20:16).

The psalms say the same thing David said: “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: David would not go out in another man's armor. Ask what borrowed armor you are trying to fight in, and what it would mean to go as yourself, trusting God. And ask whether your confidence rests on yourself, or on what God has already done.

passages.t: A stone, and a question about David's father
passages.happening:
As Goliath comes forward, David runs to meet him. He takes out a stone and slings it, and it strikes the Philistine in the forehead. ‘The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground’ (verse 49). ‘Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him’ (verse 50). David takes Goliath's own sword and cuts off his head, and the Philistines run (verse 51).

Israel and Judah chase them to the gates of Gath and Ekron, and then plunder their camp (verses 52-53). David brings the head to Jerusalem and keeps Goliath's weapons in his own tent (verse 54).

As Saul watched David go out, he had asked Abner, the commander of his army, “Abner, whose son is this young man?” (verse 55). Abner did not know. When David comes back, still holding the head, Abner brings him to Saul. “Whose son are you, young man?” asked Saul. “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem,” David replied (verse 58).
passages.hearers:
The narrator tells the killing briefly and turns to what follows: the Philistines run, and Israel finds its courage again.

Verse 54 says David brought the head to Jerusalem, a city not yet in Israel's hands. Many take this as the narrator looking ahead to what David would later do there.

The ending turns the story toward David's family and his future place in the kingdom. Saul asks whose son he is. With a royal marriage and freedom from taxes promised to the victor's family, the question may be about more than a name.
passages.later:
Jerusalem was taken from the Jebusites only later, in David's reign: ‘David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)’ (2 Samuel 5:7).

The New Testament names David among those ‘who through faith conquered kingdoms’ and ‘became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight’ (Hebrews 11:33-34).
passages.hard:
Why does Saul ask who David is, when David was already his harpist and armor-bearer in chapter 16?

Readers have noticed this for centuries, and several answers are offered. Some suggest that Saul, tormented and distracted, simply did not recognize a young court musician, or that David had been home with the flocks long enough to have grown and changed. Others point out that Saul asks whose son David is, not what his name is. With a royal marriage and freedom from taxes promised to the victor's family, Saul may be asking about David's father and household. Many scholars think the chapter keeps two accounts of how David came to Saul's notice, which the editor set side by side. The shorter form of the chapter in the oldest Greek manuscripts, which lacks verses 55 to 58, is sometimes cited in support.

These readings are not all exclusive, and the text does not settle the question. The story's main claims about God and David do not depend on which is right.
passages.asks: After the victory Saul asked whose son David was. Ask what you know about the people God has used in your life, and their families and stories. And ask whether you give God the credit for victories, as David said he would, before and after the stone is thrown.
